content.value: Instantiate objects using matching constructors; trace reference assignment and reassignment; distinguish aliases from separate instances.

An object is instantiated with new and a constructor call. The constructor initializes the object, and the expression supplies a reference that can be stored in a compatible variable. A declaration alone does not create an object. Consult the constructor’s parameter list and preconditions before calling it.

Reference assignment copies an address-like reference value. It does not duplicate the object. If two variables alias a mutable object, a mutation through one is visible through the other. Reassigning one variable affects only that variable. A reference can be null; ensure an object exists before calling its instance methods.

Initially a and b identify the first Point, while c identifies a second Point with the same coordinate values. After a = c, a and c identify the second object; b still identifies the first. Exactly two constructor calls occurred.

Do not assume matching constructor arguments make objects identical. Do not use a constructor name as though it were an ordinary method on an existing object. The types and order of arguments must match a constructor the class actually provides.

After the example, execute c = null. Which references still identify an object? Answer: a identifies the second Point and b the first; only c is null. Explain why neither object is reset by that assignment.
